You're researching a cost-cutting question for Nxeon, a game/VPS hosting platform (code at /opt/nxeon, TypeScript/Next.js/Prisma). The owner currently gives every paid game-server order a dedicated IPv4 address, and dedicated IPv4s are eating into margins (IPv4 leasing/purchase cost per address, ongoing). They want to know: for each game we sell hosting for, can the customer's server be reached WITHOUT a dedicated IPv4 — i.e. routed off a single shared IP via a subdomain/hostname, the same way Nxeon's existing FREE Minecraft tier already works?

Context on the existing pattern (read these to understand it fully before researching, don't guess):
- /opt/nxeon/lib/games.ts and /opt/nxeon/lib/game-config.ts — the full list of supported game families/tiers (grep for GAME_META, GAME_FAMILY, or similar — this is the definitive list of games to research, don't rely on my memory of what's offered).
- Search the codebase (grep -ri "mc-router\|freemc" /opt/nxeon) for how the free Minecraft tier does subdomain routing without a dedicated IP per server — it uses a Docker + mc-router setup with auto-sleep/wake, routing by SNI-like hostname on port 25565. Read whatever setup/deploy scripts or docs describe this (check /opt/nxeon for a freemc-host related directory, docker-compose, or admin panel code) so you understand exactly what technique is already proven in production, not just in theory.

Your job: for EVERY game family Nxeon currently sells (from lib/games.ts / lib/game-config.ts), determine and report:
1. Does this game's client/server protocol support a hostname-based SRV record or virtual-host style routing (like Minecraft's `_minecraft._tcp` SRV record, which lets `play.example.com` resolve to `realhost:25565` without the player ever typing a port)? Minecraft (Java) is the one confirmed case — check whether Bedrock, and every other game family in our catalog, has anything equivalent. Most Source-engine / Steam-networking games (CS2, Rust, ARK, Valheim, Palworld, 7 Days to Die, Conan Exiles, etc.) do NOT support SRV-style hostname routing because Steam's server browser and game clients connect directly to IP:port — verify this per-game rather than assuming, since it directly changes what's sellable.
2. If SRV/hostname routing isn't supported, is there a cheaper middle ground than one-dedicated-IPv4-per-customer? E.g.: a single shared IPv4 with each customer server bound to a distinct high port (port-based multiplexing instead of one-IP-per-server) — note any games whose protocol breaks with non-default ports (some Steam games query a fixed port range or need port to equal the query port + offset).
3. For games that flatly require a dedicated IP with the DEFAULT port (no port remapping tolerated), say so plainly.

Produce a table: Game | Needs dedicated IPv4? (yes/no/partial) | Why | Alternative (subdomain-SRV / shared-IP+custom-port / none). Use WebSearch to verify protocol behavior per game engine family (Source/GoldSrc, Unreal, proprietary) rather than guessing — cite what you found. Keep the final report under 600 words plus the table. This is research only — do not write or edit any code.

/** Families whose OsTemplate rows are game servers. Plain module (safe to import
 *  from server components and "use server" action files alike). */
export const GAME_FAMILIES = ["minecraft", "valheim", "rust", "palworld", "cs2", "terraria", "ark", "satisfactory", "projectzomboid", "sdtd", "vrising", "enshrouded", "factorio", "gmod", "conan", "unturned", "theforest", "sonsoftheforest", "bedrock"] as const;
export type GameFamily = (typeof GAME_FAMILIES)[number];

/**
 * Canonical display name + glyph per family, ALL 19 — the single source of truth
 * for capitalization (e.g. "Garry's Mod", "7 Days to Die", "ARK: Survival
 * Evolved", never a raw lowercase slug). Plain module, so unlike
 * components/marketing/GameLogo.tsx's GAME_VISUAL (which is "use client" and
 * also carries brand gradient colors) this is safe to import from a SERVER
 * component too.
 *
 * FIXED 2026-08-23: the deploy wizard's game picker (app/dashboard/deploy/page.tsx)
 * and the "manage my servers" list (app/dashboard/games/page.tsx) each kept their
 * OWN copy-pasted map with only 6 of 19 games — every other family silently fell
 * back to its raw slug ("sdtd", "gmod", "theforest"...) with no capitalization at
 * all. Both now import this instead of maintaining their own list.
 */
export const GAME_DISPLAY: Record<GameFamily, { name: string; glyph: string }> = {
  minecraft: { name: "Minecraft", glyph: "⛏️" },
  valheim: { name: "Valheim", glyph: "🪓" },
  rust: { name: "Rust", glyph: "🔧" },
  palworld: { name: "Palworld", glyph: "🐾" },
  cs2: { name: "Counter-Strike 2", glyph: "🎯" },
  terraria: { name: "Terraria", glyph: "🌳" },
  ark: { name: "ARK: Survival Evolved", glyph: "🦖" },
  satisfactory: { name: "Satisfactory", glyph: "🏭" },
  projectzomboid: { name: "Project Zomboid", glyph: "🧟" },
  sdtd: { name: "7 Days to Die", glyph: "🪓" },
  vrising: { name: "V Rising", glyph: "🩸" },
  enshrouded: { name: "Enshrouded", glyph: "🌫️" },
  factorio: { name: "Factorio", glyph: "🏭" },
  gmod: { name: "Garry's Mod", glyph: "🧰" },
  conan: { name: "Conan Exiles", glyph: "🗡️" },
  unturned: { name: "Unturned", glyph: "🏝️" },
  theforest: { name: "The Forest", glyph: "🌲" },
  sonsoftheforest: { name: "Sons of the Forest", glyph: "🪚" },
  bedrock: { name: "Minecraft Bedrock", glyph: "🧱" },
};

/**
 * Family id → art slug for the real key-art bundled at
 * public/games/art/<slug>_poster.jpg and public/games/art/<slug>_hero.jpg
 * (naming differs from the family id for a few titles). Single source of truth
 * for every consumer (GameCoverCarousel, GameCoverTile, GameHero) — was
 * previously copy-pasted separately in GameCoverCarousel.tsx, which is exactly
 * the kind of drift that caused the GAME_DISPLAY capitalization bug above.
 *
 * `poster` is omitted for minecraft (no poster art was provided — it resolves
 * real cover art via a different fallback chain instead). Every family has a
 * `hero`.
 */
/**
 * Family id → the port a customer's game client actually connects to, plus
 * which transport it is reachable on. This is the single source of truth for
 * `worker/provision-health.ts`'s post-boot game-port verification (added after
 * a Terraria order silently sat on an interactive world-selection prompt with
 * no TTY — the container showed "Up" while nothing ever bound the port, and
 * PROVISION reported success anyway).
 *
 * SOURCED DIRECTLY from each family's `docker run -p ...` mapping in
 * prisma/catalog.ts / prisma/seed-wave1-games.ts / prisma/seed-wave2-games.ts —
 * these are the ONLY ports Docker actually exposes off the container, so they
 * are the only ports reachable from outside it. If a game's setup script ever
 * changes its `-p` mapping, this entry must change with it or the health check
 * will probe a port nothing forwards to.
 *
 * `protocol` is not always the game's own play port: several titles (valheim,
 * palworld, vrising, enshrouded, theforest, sonsoftheforest, bedrock) expose
 * ONLY a UDP port in their image — no TCP port is mapped at all, so there is
 * nothing a TCP connect could ever prove for them. Where an image also exposes
 * a TCP port (often RCON/query, e.g. rust's 28016, ark's 27020, factorio's
 * 27015) THAT port is used instead: a TCP handshake is verifiable with a plain
 * connect, and the process binding it is proof the game server itself came up,
 * which is exactly the class of bug this check exists to catch — even though
 * it isn't the port the player's game client uses to join.
 */

  minecraft: { port: 25565, protocol: "tcp" },
  valheim: { port: 2456, protocol: "udp" }, // no tcp port mapped
  rust: { port: 28016, protocol: "tcp" }, // rcon tcp; 28015/udp is the join port
  palworld: { port: 8211, protocol: "udp" }, // no tcp port mapped

  enshrouded: { port: 15636, protocol: "udp" }, // no tcp port mapped
  factorio: { port: 27015, protocol: "tcp" }, // rcon tcp; 34197/udp is the join port
  gmod: { port: 27015, protocol: "tcp" },
  conan: { port: 7777, protocol: "tcp" }, // image maps 7777 as both tcp+udp
  unturned: { port: 27015, protocol: "tcp" }, // 27015-27017 mapped as both tcp+udp
  theforest: { port: 27015, protocol: "udp" }, // no tcp port mapped
  sonsoftheforest: { port: 8766, protocol: "udp" }, // no tcp port mapped
  bedrock: { port: 19132, protocol: "udp" }, // RakNet — no tcp variant exists
};

Bedrock Edition does not support SRV records. For Bedrock, use an A record pointing to your IP and specify the port in the client.

## How mc-router Works

mc-router is a lightweight connection multiplexer that routes TCP traffic based on the server address (hostname) in the initial Minecraft handshake. This allows hosting multiple servers on a single public IP.

## The Protocol & Handshake Process

The client initiates the connection with the gateway and sends a Handshake packet immediately followed by a Login Start packet as it does with every server. The gateway reads these packets, extracts the server address field and finds the corresponding server. Once found, the gateway initiates a connection with the server, sends those same packets it received prior, and then pipes the two connections together so that every data received from the client is sent to the server, and every data sent by the server is sent to the client.

## Hostname Mapping

The mapping declares how the hostname users will enter into their Minecraft client will map to the internal services. The router can work with any hostname as long as its DNS record points to the router.

## SRV Records Support

mc-router includes support for SRV records, with an option to "simplify fully qualified SRV records for mapping" (controlled by the `-simplify-srv` flag). A Service record (SRV record) is a specification of data in the Domain Name System defining the location, i.e., the hostname and port number, of servers for specified services. This allows clients to discover the correct server address and port through DNS rather than hardcoding them.

## Research summary

**How the free-tier Minecraft pattern actually works** (confirmed in `/opt/nxeon/lib/free-minecraft-control.ts`, `lib/actions-free-minecraft.ts`, `lib/freemc-capacity.ts`): a single shared IP runs `itzg/mc-router`, a Go proxy that reads the **server-address field inside Minecraft's own handshake packet** (like an HTTP Host header / TLS SNI, not DNS) and pipes the connection to whichever container's Docker label (`mc-router.host=<subdomain>.<domain>`) matches. Nxeon additionally publishes a `_minecraft._tcp` **DNS SRV record** so players can type a bare hostname with no port and still land on port 25565. Both pieces — SRV (for the port) and handshake vhosting (for routing multiple backends off one IP) — are Minecraft-Java-protocol-specific. No other game in the catalog has an equivalent handshake field or SRV convention; this was verified per-engine-family via web search, not assumed.

19 families are catalogued in `/opt/nxeon/lib/games.ts` (`GAME_FAMILIES`/`GAME_PORT`). Findings:

| Game | Needs dedicated IPv4? | Why | Alternative |
|---|---|---|---|
| Minecraft (Java) | No | SRV + mc-router handshake vhosting — already proven in prod | subdomain-SRV (shipped) |
| Minecraft Bedrock | Partial | RakNet/UDP; Bedrock client has **no SRV support** — confirmed: player must type literal IP:port, no hostname-only entry | shared-IP + custom port (works, just not zero-config) |
| CS2 | Partial | Source engine; Steam browser/direct-connect always use raw IP:port, no SRV | shared-IP + custom port (huge existing precedent — most community CS servers already run on non-default ports) |
| Garry's Mod | Partial | Same Source engine model as CS2 | shared-IP + custom port |
| Rust | Partial | Steam-networked, no SRV; port fully configurable via `server.port` | shared-IP + custom port |
| Palworld | Partial | No SRV; needs both `-port` and `-QueryPort` set per instance (older builds lacked a configurable query port — now fixed) | shared-IP + custom port |
| ARK: Survival Evolved | Partial | Unreal+Steam; no SRV; needs a distinct game port **and** query port pair per instance | shared-IP + custom port-pair (convention: step by 10/5) |
| Satisfactory | Partial | Unreal; no Steam server browser (invite/direct-IP model); `-Port=` fully configurable | shared-IP + custom port |
| Project Zomboid | Partial | No SRV; `DefaultPort` configurable | shared-IP + custom port |
| 7 Days to Die | Partial | No SRV; uses a **contiguous TCP+UDP block** (26900-26903 by default) that can be shifted as a whole per instance | shared-IP + custom port-block |
| V Rising | Partial | Unreal-family, no SRV; game port + query port (conventionally +1) both configurable | shared-IP + custom port-pair |
| Enshrouded | Partial | Proprietary; single UDP port, direct-connect only, no SRV | shared-IP + custom port |
| Factorio | Partial | Proprietary, single UDP port, no query-port coupling at all — most port-flexible title in the catalog | shared-IP + custom port |
| Conan Exiles | Partial | Unreal+Steam; game+query port pair, no SRV | shared-IP + custom port-pair |
| Unturned | Partial | Unity+Steam; 3-port set (game/query/workshop), no SRV | shared-IP + custom port-set |
| The Forest | Partial | Proprietary Endnight engine, Steam-networked, no SRV | shared-IP + custom port |
| Sons of the Forest | Partial | Same engine family as The Forest | shared-IP + custom port |
| Terraria | Partial | Proprietary raw TCP socket, no query protocol, no SRV — arguably the most flexible non-Minecraft title | shared-IP + custom port (trivial) |

**Bottom line:** Minecraft Java is the only family with true zero-dedicated-IP, zero-custom-port subdomain routing. Bedrock and all 17 remaining families are "no SRV, but no fixed-port requirement either" — every one of them tolerated a non-default port in the sources checked, so **shared-IP + per-customer high port** is a viable dedicated-IPv4 replacement across the entire non-Minecraft catalog. The only added complexity is that several titles (ARK, 7DTD, V Rising, Unturned, Palworld) need a *pair or block* of ports moved together per instance rather than a single port, and Bedrock/Steam-browser games lose the "just type a hostname" convenience — customers get `ip:port` instead of `sub.nxeon.cloud`, which is a UX/support-load tradeoff worth flagging to the owner, not a technical blocker. Firewall/NAT rules would need to move from "one IP, default port" to "shared IP, per-order port allocation" in the provisioning worker, but no game in the catalog outright *requires* a dedicated IP at the protocol level.
